Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated description: brightly evident (昭昭) and keenly numinous or responsive (靈靈), hence "bright and numinous." It occurs 240 times in 101 allowlisted texts. Chinese Chan records frequently use the phrase while rejecting its identification with one's true self. One address asks, "if you recognize the bright and numinous as your reality, why does it no longer remain bright and numinous when you are asleep?" (汝若認昭昭靈靈是汝真實，為甚麼瞌睡時又不成昭昭靈靈). The same address gives a direct account: the bright and numinous arises because colors, sounds, scents, and other things before one are distinguished; without those things it is like "turtle fur and rabbit horns" (昭昭靈靈，祇因前塵色聲香等法而有分別；若無前塵，同於龜毛兔角). Another record states that the fault lies in taking the presently bright and numinous as correct, since it "arises dependent on encountered objects" (昭昭靈靈乃是緣境而有). These are the corpus's explicit predicates, not an entry-level theory of consciousness.
Senses.Note: The phrase also appears in first-person retrospective description. One speaker says he was still "hazy and indistinct, bright and numinous, and had not yet obtained stability" (恍恍惚惚、昭昭靈靈，也未得個安穩); a later account says that this bright-and-numinous condition could not be made to arise and could not be found after a subsequent event. A verse asks, "what is the bright and numinous? By the time you blink, it has already been missed" (昭昭靈靈是什麼？眨得眼來已蹉過). Productive forms include "the bright-and-numinous one" (昭昭靈靈底, 14 occurrences in 12 texts) and "recognize the bright and numinous" (認昭昭靈靈, 21 in 16). Eight texts preserve the sleep challenge's wording "the bright and numinous is your reality" (昭昭靈靈是汝真實).

Occurrences.Kwic: 我今問汝：汝若認昭昭靈靈是汝真實，為甚麼瞌睡時又不成昭昭靈靈？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct challenge: if you recognize the bright and numinous as your reality, why is it no longer bright and numinous while asleep?

Occurrences.Kwic: 我向汝道：昭昭靈靈，祇因前塵色聲香等法而有分別，便道此是昭昭靈靈。若無前塵，汝此昭昭靈靈同於龜毛兔角。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The address explicitly relates bright-and-numinous distinction to colors, sounds, scents, and other encountered things; without them it compares the phrase to turtle fur and rabbit horns.

Occurrences.Kwic: 病在認目前昭昭靈靈以為是，不知昭昭靈靈乃是緣境而有。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later address calls recognizing the presently bright and numinous as correct a fault and says it arises dependent on encountered objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然如是，只是恍恍惚惚、昭昭靈靈，也未得個安穩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: First-person retrospective: despite the preceding encounter, the speaker remained hazy and indistinct, bright and numinous, and had not yet obtained stability.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昭昭靈靈是什麼？眨得眼來已蹉過。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Verse question: what is the bright and numinous? By the time one blinks, it has already been missed.

RelatedTerms: turtle fur and rabbit horns (龜毛兔角)

Senses.PreferredTarget: put another head atop one's head
AlternateTargets: add a head on top of the head
set a head upon one's head
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "put another head atop one's head." The idiom occurs 280 times in 141 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it as a verdict when a speaker adds a name, assertion, attainment, or further operation to what the passage says is already present. Linji follows it with the question, "what do you lack?" (是儞欠少甚麼). Another record pairs "you have finished eating gruel—putting another head atop your head" (喫粥了也，頭上安頭) with "go wash your bowl—drawing feet on a snake" (洗鉢盂去，為蛇畫足). Other explicit parallels are "add frost atop snow" (霜加雪上) and "put a shackle on a cangue" (枷上著杻). These corpus comparisons establish unnecessary addition without importing an external theory.
Senses.Note: The phrase is productive in binary naming tests: calling an object a staff may be "putting another head atop one's head," while denying it is a staff may be "cutting off the head to seek life" (斬頭覓活). Saying "mind itself is Buddha" (即心是佛) is likewise compared to putting another head atop one's head, while saying "neither mind nor Buddha" (非心非佛) is compared to losing the head and recognizing its shadow (迷頭認影). One community address explicitly lists "do not put another head atop your head" (不得頭上安頭) as the fourth of four ailments, after seeking another's spittle along the road, driving a stake while rocking an oar, and cutting off the head to seek life. The term names none of those other expressions; their value here is the corpus's own contrast set.

Occurrences.Kwic: 瞎漢頭上安頭，是儞欠少甚麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's direct wording: blind fellows put another head atop their heads; what do you lack?

Occurrences.Kwic: 第四不得頭上安頭。能離四病，自然天下太平。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is explicitly the fourth of four ailments: do not put another head atop your head; if one can leave the four ailments, all under heaven is naturally at peace.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：喫粥了也，頭上安頭。洗鉢盂去，為虵畫足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Corpus-native comparison: having finished gruel is followed by putting a head atop the head; going to wash the bowl is followed by drawing feet on a snake.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若向這裏說即心是佛，大似頭上安頭；若說非心非佛，何異迷頭認影？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Saying mind itself is Buddha is compared to putting another head atop one's head; saying neither mind nor Buddha is compared to losing the head and recognizing its shadow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉拳曰：還見麼？師曰：見。悟曰：頭上安頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In an encounter, Yuanwu raises his fist and asks whether it is seen; the answer yes receives the verdict putting another head atop one's head.

RelatedTerms: draw feet on a snake (為蛇畫足)
cut off the head to seek life (斬頭覓活)
add frost atop snow (霜加雪上)
put a shackle on a cangue (枷上著杻)
